problem: 'Lower f at the same V saves little energy per operation' is wrong. Dynamic energy per operation is E_op = α × C × V², which does not contain f at all. Lowering f at constant V reduces power (P = αCV²f) but saves no switching energy per operation, and can raise total energy because the block runs longer and leaks for longer.
fix: Write: 'Lowering f at the same V cuts power but not the dynamic energy per operation, because E_op = α × C × V² has no f in it; the block simply takes longer. Lowering V saves real energy because E_op falls with V². The catch is that a lower V needs a lower f to stay stable, so DVFS changes both together.'

problem: 'Stop its clock until the interrupt arrives' is stated as a guarantee. WFI is only a hint: the architecture says execution suspends until an interrupt is taken, and the chip decides what low-power state (if any) is entered. If an interrupt is already pending, WFI completes immediately.
fix: Answer: 'WFI asks the core to suspend execution until an interrupt is taken. The chip may then stop the core clock or enter a deeper low-power state; WFI is a hint, so the exact action is implementation-defined.'

problem: The charge is left in mA·ms only. Students cannot judge whether 200.45 mA·ms is a sane number, and the unit looks unusual on an answer sheet.
fix: Add: 1 mA·ms = 1 µC, so 200.45 mA·ms = 200.45 µC of charge per cycle. State the answer as '200.45 µC (200.45 mA·ms)'.

problem: 'Reduces both switching energy and frequency' is muddled: cutting frequency does not itself save energy. The saving comes from V², and the frequency cut is what keeps the circuit stable at the lower V.
fix: Answer: 'Dynamic energy per operation is α × C × V², so lowering V cuts energy quadratically. Lowering f alone cuts power but not energy per operation, and leakage makes it worse over a longer run. DVFS lowers V and f together to keep timing stable, so it saves energy and power.'
